title: A tap and a tub
hook: You overspend $200 a month. How big is the debt after six months?

doesNotKnow: that a deficit is an amount per period (a flow) and debt is the running total (a stock)

misconception: A deficit and a debt are the same thing.
objective: The learner can explain that a $200 monthly deficit added to a $1,000 debt gives $2,200 after six months, and that debt falls only in months when the gap turns negative.

claims.text: Owing $1,000 and spending $200 more than you earn each month for 6 months leaves $2,200 owed, ignoring interest.
The $200 is a deficit, an amount per month (a flow); the $2,200 is the debt, an accumulated total (a stock).
claims.source: Standard stock-flow definitions: a flow is measured per period, a stock at a point in time (Mankiw, Principles of Economics; national debt vs budget deficit).

claims.text: A month in which you save $200 lowers the debt by $200; debt only falls when the monthly gap is negative.
claims.source: level(next) = level + gap (Demo.tsx levelAfter()); a negative gap lowers the level.

claims.text: With interest the tap would grow, because interest is added to the debt on top of the gap.
claims.source: Interest on a positive debt is a further inflow each month; this stage ignores it.

claims.text: The lesson is a model: the tub is an analogy, there is no interest, and debt in the stage cannot fall below $0.
claims.source: Stage chip 'Model: no interest; the tap is spending minus income'; Demo.tsx levelAfter() floors at 0.

recall.question: A household has a budget deficit of $100 each month for a year. Which statement is right?
options: Its debt grows by $1,200 over the year
recall.why: The deficit is a flow of $100 per month; twelve months add 12 x $100 = $1,200 to the debt (ignoring interest).
